parameterNotes.dependency: the feed that changed what a field means; the mismatch share belongs to the consumer, so the feed is the mechanism rather than the subject of a reading.
parameterNotes.changedField: the field whose meaning changed while its name stayed; the field-count series says a field was added, not which one changed.
parameterNotes.addedField: the field added beside it, which is what makes the change additive and therefore invisible to a parser that only checks for absence.

groundTruth.rootCauseReason: The feed changed what one field means while leaving its name alone: `rate` was the exact ratio and is now the same ratio rounded to two places, and `inverse` was added beside it. A consumer cannot detect that from the outside -- the key exists, its type is unchanged, and its value is still a plausible number -- so every reader of `rate` inherited a rounding error it had no way to refuse. Settlement is the reader, not the answer: its parser does exactly what the contract it was written against says, and the two-hour window is the deploy's, not the parser's. The deploy is the timestamp of the defect rather than its cause, which is the distinction this annotation keeps: a case that named the deploy would be answerable from a release log without reading what changed in the payload.

rootCauseIndicators.description: the shape of the response, which is the only reading on the feed that moved: one field before the change and two after
the share of orders whose total disagreed by cents, which is a property of the reader and therefore points away from the answer
the parser naming the field it read and what the feed now does to it, which is the only reading that says "rounded" in words

causalChain.mechanism: the release changes what the serialiser writes into one existing key: the exact ratio became a two-place approximation, and a second key was added beside it, so the payload is wider by one field and less precise by an amount the reader cannot see

every replica runs the release, so every caller receives the new shape at once and none of them receives the old one; the feed answers every request successfully, at its usual rate and latency, which is why nothing measured at the feed's edge looks wrong

settlement reads `rate` as the contract says and multiplies, so a rate that is off by less than a cent in the feed becomes a total that is off by a cent or two; the calls all succeed, no timeout is logged, and the only visible symptom is that a share of the totals on the settlement side disagree with the same totals computed before the change

evidenceCheckpoints.description: the share of orders whose stored total differs from the total recomputed at the pre-change rate, which is the symptom and not the cause: it is a property of the reader
the number of fields the rate object carries, which is the only thing on the feed that moved: one before the change, two after
the window the injection declared, which is the two hours between the deploy at 09:00 and the revert at 11:00 -- the same interval the incident text states twice

evidenceCheckpoints.value: the feed rounds to two places
evidenceCheckpoints.description: the parser's own line, which names the field it read and the rounding it inherited: the only reading that turns "wrong by a few cents" into a mechanism rather than a magnitude

remediation.action: carry the new field additively and keep the old one exact, or put a version on the payload so a consumer can refuse a shape it was not written for -- a field whose meaning changes under its own name is undetectable downstream
assert the response shape settlement depends on, so a narrowing of a field it reads is a startup failure rather than a cent-sized error in every total

sli.none: the mismatch is read as a share of settlements that disagree and a count of response fields, and the answer key’s own component contributes only the count: it carries no duration.

query: Settlement totals were wrong by a few cents for two hours while every call to the currency feed succeeded. Which component changed, and why did nothing in the settlement service's own telemetry look wrong?
